agent_notes: The 'you' in lakh (to you) is masculine, so the poet turns back to the king; the shift from the queen (feminine 'your face', v. 13) to the king is abrupt, and the STEPBible gloss for this word is right. The lamed of lirkamot is read as 'in' (so Radak, Ibn Ezra, Meiri); I rendered it 'to' in layer 1 to show the preposition as written and mentioned the other reading in the commentary.

agent_notes: The speaker of azkirah ('I will cause to be remembered') and the addressee of shimkha are disputed in the classical commentaries (Ibn Ezra lists two views; Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David take the king to be the Messiah, or God). I read the poet addressing the king, as in the frame of v. 2 where the poet's tongue is a scribe's pen, and said so in the commentary.
Rashi on this verse and 45:18 only says the poet speaks 'toward the Holy One'; I cite it only as a reading and do not rest any claim on it.

STEPBible glosses yafeyafita 'you are handsome'; the doubled-root intensive is better 'beautiful beyond measure'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri debate whether the doubling intensifies; I followed the intensive reading.

agent_notes: The crux of the window. Hebrew kis'akha 'elohim 'olam va'ed can be read as 'Your throne, O God, is forever' (vocative, KJV/ASV/YLT/BBE all agree), 'your throne is a throne of God', or 'God [is/establishes] your throne' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri as quoted in the packet). The literal layer keeps the vocative with the ambiguity flagged in the commentary; I did not choose between readings beyond that. The STEPBible entity tag deity.yhwh on 'elohim is a registry guess for a possibly human-addressed word.

agent_notes: minni is unclear: 'stringed instruments' (STEPBible, KJV-family), 'from which' with an extra yod (Radak, Metzudat Zion in the packet), or a place name (Ibn Ezra rejects it). notes.note: Traditional commentaries in the packet read the psalm as addressed to Solomon, David or the Messiah, with the bride as a convert or Israel. The Hebrew itself names none of them, and I kept the drama within the text: a poet, a king and a bride. Where the commentaries diverge I cited them rather than adopting one.
